beats.narration: Begin by framing Problem Statement and Algorithmic Foundations as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Consider this worked case: A student defines a sorting problem by listing input arrays and expected sorted outputs before writing any code. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Problem Statement and Algorithmic Foundations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a split-screen: left side shows a textual problem statement with input/output examples; right side shows a flowchart of the algorithmic steps.

beats.narration: Now define Data Representation: Lists, Stacks, and Queues precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Consider this worked case: A stack of plates is added and removed only from the top, while a line of people waiting for a bus is processed from the front. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Data Representation: Lists, Stacks, and Queues
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Animate three separate diagrams: a linear list with indices, a stack with arrows pointing only to the top element, and a queue with arrows entering at the tail and leaving at the head.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Hierarchical and Connected Structures operates in a concrete sequence. Topics include tree and graph structures, nested data structures, objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces, object-oriented collection class libraries for abstract data types (for example stacks, queues, maps, and trees), and static versus dynamic data types. Consider this worked case: A family tree illustrates hierarchical relationships, while a subway map illustrates a graph of connected stations. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Hierarchical and Connected Structures
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a binary tree diagram with labeled nodes and edges, followed by a directed graph with multiple cycles and labeled vertices.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Objects, Classes, and Inheritance and make the decision criteria explicit. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Consider this worked case: A 'Dog' class inherits from an 'Animal' class, gaining shared attributes like 'name' while adding specific ones like 'bark'. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Objects, Classes, and Inheritance
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a UML class diagram with an 'Animal' superclass and a 'Dog' subclass, highlighting the inheritance arrow and instance attributes.

beats.narration: Apply Software Qualities: Cohesion and Coupling to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Software qualities related to object orientation, namely cohesion, minimal coupling, modifiability, and extensibility, are all introduced in this course, as well as a few elementary object-oriented design patterns. Consider this worked case: A 'PaymentProcessor' class has high cohesion because it handles only payment logic, and low coupling because it does not directly access database tables. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Software Qualities: Cohesion and Coupling
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present two side-by-side code snippets: one tightly coupled with multiple imports and direct variable access, and one loosely coupled using interfaces or abstract classes.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Abstract Data Types and Collection Libraries, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. This accelerated course covers material from the first-year sequence of courses and provides the foundation for all subsequent Computer Science courses. Consider this worked case: Using Python's collections module, a developer instantiates a deque as a stack or a defaultdict as a map without writing low-level logic. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Abstract Data Types and Collection Libraries
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a table listing Python collection classes (e.g., list, deque, dict, defaultdict) with brief descriptions of their primary operations.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Exception Handling and Control Flow with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. Consider this worked case: A division-by-zero error is caught by a try/except block that logs the error and returns a default value instead of crashing. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Exception Handling and Control Flow
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Animate a program execution trace where a normal flow is interrupted by an exception, jumps to a handler block, and then resumes.

beats.narration: Use Input and Output Streams to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Input and output streams, graphical user interfaces, and exception handling are covered. Consider this worked case: A program reads a text file using sys. stdin and writes formatted results to a log file using open('log. txt', 'w'). Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Input and Output Streams
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a diagram with arrows labeled 'read' entering a buffer and 'write' exiting to a file icon, alongside code snippets for both operations.

beats.narration: Connect Graphical User Interfaces to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. The course stresses problem solving while covering modern software development techniques and introducing essential software tools. Consider this worked case: A simple GUI window displays a button; clicking the button triggers a function that updates a label on the screen. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Graphical User Interfaces
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a mockup of a window with a button and a label, then highlight the button press event and the subsequent label update.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases. Consider this worked case: A developer writes unit tests for a sorting function, traces its execution on an empty list and a reversed list, and fixes a bug where the loop condition fails at the boundary. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a checklist graphic with four items: 'Write Tests', 'Trace Execution', 'Identify Boundary Cases', 'Debug and Verify', each accompanied by a small icon.

sources.excerpt: The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. sources.excerpt: Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.
